text: In normal air at 1 atm the computed flame temperatures are methane 2225 K, heptane 2274 K and methanol 2220 K.
Against NASA's own flame temperatures in PSI-10 our values are off by 2.5 K at the median and 8.9 K at worst over 147 flames (mean 2456 K ours against 2454 K NASA's).
Heat conduction of pure nitrogen, carbon dioxide and helium at 300 K is within 10% of textbook values (0.0264, 0.0175 and 0.1545 W/(m K)).
On tests from days it never saw, the two numbers explain 72% of the variation in fuel burned (error about 13 points), against 4% for the oxygen level alone.
Trained on nitrogen-only tests, ceiling temperature predicts burning rate in carbon dioxide tests (R2 0.47) better than the oxygen level does (R2 0.05).
For methanol tests with helium, temperature alone fails (R2 -0.34); adding heat-spreading speed gives R2 0.16, so helium is not explained by temperature alone.
Near-identical tests end 7.1 points apart in share of fuel burned (median), the noise floor for any model.
273 of the 274 FLEX tests have both computed numbers; one test (114) lists a pressure of 0 and is left out.
The coldest heptane mixture (nitrogen only) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 1770 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The coldest heptane mixture (with carbon dioxide) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 1764 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The coldest heptane mixture (with helium) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 2092 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The coldest methanol mixture (nitrogen only) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 1674 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The coldest methanol mixture (with carbon dioxide) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 1627 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The coldest methanol mixture (with helium) that still gave a recorded test has a ceiling temperature of 1916 K; this is the edge of what was tested, not a measured limit.
The fitted link is off by about 13 points of fuel burned on unseen test days.

In PSI's per-test droplet tables (FLEX PSI-69, CFI PSI-39) no diluted test sits above 25% oxygen. FLEX-2 (PSI-68) lists helium mixtures up to 30% oxygen as its planned range, but PSI holds no per-test rows to say which flew. Carbon dioxide dilution above 25% oxygen appears in none of the three.
unit: mole fraction of oxygen (highest among diluted per-test rows)

text: Flown as one designed batch, 6 tests would leave no condition at 30 to 34% oxygen farther than 0.24 of a slider width from a test (today: 0.76). The first 6 conditions of a one-by-one ranking would leave 0.45. This is coverage of the tested conditions, not a prediction of what a flame would do.
unit: slider widths (largest gap left after 6 tests)

text: On unseen test days the model misses by about 1.9 times the scatter between repeated tests (16.6 against 8.8 points; 95% interval 1.3 to 3.3, from 24 pairs). About 28% of its squared error is scatter no model could remove; the rest is something the two physical numbers do not capture.
unit: times the scatter between repeated tests

text: Replayed on tests already flown: with the 94 tests with carbon dioxide treated as never flown, the model is 18.0 points off on them. Handed back as a designed batch they leave it 15.1 points off on average over batch sizes 1 to 30, against 17.1 for the top of a one-by-one ranking and 12.8 with every test handed back. The batch was ahead of the ranking in 2 of 3 replays; it was behind for tests with helium.
unit: points of fuel burned (mean error over batch sizes 1 to 30)
